facts: Chester has the most complete set of medieval city walls in Britain, forming a full circuit of about two miles.
The Chester Rows are a unique two-tier system of covered medieval shopping galleries.
Chester was founded as a Roman fortress, Deva Victrix, around 79 AD.
Shrewsbury sits almost entirely encircled by a loop of the River Severn, giving it a naturally defensible shape.
Naturalist Charles Darwin was born in Shrewsbury in 1809.
The town retains over 660 listed buildings, including many timber-framed Tudor structures.
Hereford Cathedral houses the Mappa Mundi, the largest medieval map known still to survive.
The cathedral's Chained Library preserves over 1,500 books still attached by their original chains.
Hereford is the county town of Herefordshire, on the River Wye.
Ludlow Castle was once the seat of the Council of Wales and the Marches.
Ludlow has become renowned as a food destination, once hosting more Michelin-starred restaurants per head than any UK town.
The town's medieval street layout survives almost unchanged.
Stokesay Castle is regarded as the finest and best-preserved fortified manor house in England.
It was built in the late 13th century by a wealthy wool merchant, Laurence of Ludlow.
Craven Arms sits at a key crossroads in south Shropshire.
Knighton is considered the unofficial capital of Offa's Dyke, the 8th-century earthwork marking the Wales-England border.
The Offa's Dyke Centre in the town explains the history of this ancient boundary.
Knighton's Welsh name, Tref-y-Clawdd, means 'town on the dyke'.
Powis Castle's terraced gardens are among the finest surviving examples of a 17th-century Italianate garden in Britain.
The castle holds treasures brought back from India by Clive of India's family.
Welshpool sits in the Severn Valley, close to the English border.
Social reformer Robert Owen, a pioneer of the cooperative movement, was born in Newtown in 1771.
The town was once a major centre of the Welsh flannel and wool industry.
Newtown sits on the River Severn in mid Wales.
Conwy's town walls, built alongside the castle, remain almost entirely intact after more than 700 years.
The town is also home to the smallest house in Britain, on the quayside.
Conwy forms part of Edward I's 'Ring of Iron' of North Wales castles, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Llandudno's curving promenade, lined with Victorian hotels, remains largely unchanged since the 19th century.
The town has the longest pier in Wales, extending nearly 700 metres into the sea.
Llandudno was carefully planned from the 1850s as a purpose-built seaside resort.
Holyhead Breakwater, completed in 1873, is the longest breakwater in the United Kingdom.
Holyhead has been the main ferry gateway from Wales to Ireland since the early 19th century.
The town sits on Holy Island, off the northwest coast of Anglesey.
Bangor University, founded in 1884, was funded partly by public subscriptions from Welsh quarrymen and farmers.
Bangor is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the UK, tracing its roots to a 6th-century monastery.
The city overlooks the Menai Strait, separating the mainland from Anglesey.
Harlech Castle withstood the longest siege in British history during the Wars of the Roses.
It forms part of the same UNESCO World Heritage listing as Conwy and Caernarfon castles.
The castle sits on a rocky outcrop that once stood directly above the sea.
The Ffestiniog Railway is one of the oldest surviving narrow-gauge railways in the world, dating to 1836.
It originally carried slate down from Blaenau Ffestiniog to Porthmadog's harbour for shipping.
Porthmadog itself was built on land reclaimed from the Glaslyn estuary.
Blaenau Ffestiniog sits amid vast man-made mountains of slate waste from over a century of mining.
Underground tours take visitors deep into former slate caverns beneath the town.
The town's slate landscape forms part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Criccieth Castle was originally built by Welsh princes before being captured and strengthened by Edward I.
The town was the boyhood home of former Prime Minister David Lloyd George.
Criccieth overlooks Tremadog Bay on the Llyn Peninsula.
Barmouth's wooden railway viaduct across the Mawddach Estuary is one of the longest timber viaducts in Britain.
The town developed as a Victorian seaside resort at the mouth of the Mawddach.
Barmouth sits beneath the southern edge of the Eryri (Snowdonia) mountains.
The Talyllyn Railway, running from Tywyn, was the first railway in the world to be preserved as a heritage line, in 1951.
Tywyn is also home to the Narrow Gauge Railway Museum.
The town sits on Cardigan Bay in Gwynedd.
Aberystwyth's Cliff Railway is the longest electric cliff railway in Britain, opened in 1896.
The town's ruined castle overlooks the seafront promenade.
Aberystwyth is a major university town and cultural centre for mid Wales.
Machynlleth's Parliament House marks the traditional site of Owain Glyndwr's Welsh parliament of 1404.
The town's ornate clock tower was built in 1873 to mark a coming-of-age in the local Londonderry family.
Machynlleth sits at the head of the Dyfi Estuary.
Welsh Mountain Zoo, overlooking Colwyn Bay, specialises in conservation breeding programmes.
The town developed as a Victorian seaside resort along the North Wales coast.
Colwyn Bay sits between Llandudno and Rhyl.
Rhyl developed as one of North Wales' leading seaside resorts from the Victorian era onward.
The town's Sun Centre was one of Britain's earliest indoor water parks when it opened in the 1980s.
Rhyl sits at the mouth of the River Clwyd.
Prestatyn marks the northern end of the Offa's Dyke Path, a 177-mile route along the Wales-England border.
The town also sits at one end of the North Wales coastal path.
Prestatyn developed as a seaside resort in the 19th and 20th centuries.
Flint Castle was the first of Edward I's castles built during his conquest of Wales, begun in 1277.
Richard II was captured at Flint Castle in 1399, an event dramatised by Shakespeare.
Flint sits on the Dee Estuary in northeast Wales.
Wrexham's Racecourse Ground is recognised as the oldest international football stadium still hosting matches in the world.
Wrexham became Wales' newest city in 2022.
The city sits close to the Wales-England border, in the shadow of the Clwydian Range.
Chirk Castle has been continuously inhabited since it was completed in 1310, unusual among Welsh border castles.
The nearby Chirk Aqueduct and Viaduct carry the Llangollen Canal and railway side by side across the Ceiriog Valley.
Chirk sits right on the border between Wales and Shropshire.
The Llangollen Railway is a heritage steam line running through the scenic Dee Valley.
The nearby Pontcysyllte Aqueduct, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, carries the Llangollen Canal 38 metres above the valley.
Ruabon is the nearest mainline station, on the Wrexham to Shrewsbury line.
Nantwich has one of the best collections of black-and-white Tudor buildings in England.
The town was historically a centre of salt production, giving it the old nickname 'Wich Town'.
Nantwich's church, St Mary's, is sometimes called the 'Cathedral of South Cheshire'.

landmark: Whitchurch's clock and bell foundry heritage
facts: Whitchurch was home to a working bell and clock foundry for over 200 years, one of the oldest in Britain.
The town sits close to the Wales-England border in north Shropshire.
Whitchurch's parish church holds the tomb of John Talbot, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury.
Overton Hill, above Frodsham, offers panoramic views across the Mersey and Weaver valleys.
The town sits on the edge of the Cheshire Plain, close to the River Weaver.
Frodsham was historically a staging post on the road between Chester and Warrington.
Helsby Hill is a sandstone outcrop offering wide views across the Cheshire Plain to Wales.
The hill has evidence of an Iron Age hillfort at its summit.
Helsby sits close to the Manchester Ship Canal and the River Mersey.
Runcorn is linked to Widnes by both a road bridge and, historically, a transporter bridge across the Mersey.
The town was designated a new town in 1964, with a distinctive network of busways.
Runcorn East station sits on the edge of the town, some distance from the modern centre.
Former Prime Minister William Gladstone lived at Hawarden Castle for much of his life.
St Deiniol's Library in the village, founded by Gladstone, is Britain's only residential library.
Hawarden sits in Flintshire, close to the English border.
The village has the longest place name in the UK, often shortened from its full 58-letter Welsh form.
It sits close to the Marquess of Anglesey's Column, commemorating a Napoleonic War cavalry commander.
Llanfairpwll is on Anglesey, just across the Menai Strait from Bangor.
Valley sits close to South Stack, a dramatic sea stack and lighthouse on Anglesey's western coast.
The village takes its name from a former RAF station still active nearby.
Valley is a key stop on the Anglesey coast line towards Holyhead.
Rhosneigr is a popular centre for windsurfing and kitesurfing on Anglesey's west coast.
The village has two large sandy beaches either side of its centre.
Rhosneigr developed as a holiday destination after the railway arrived in the 1840s.
Bodorgan station serves the Bodorgan Estate, one of the largest landholdings on Anglesey.
The area is predominantly agricultural, in the interior of the island.
Bodorgan sits on the main line between Holyhead and Bangor.
Penmaen Mawr mountain was quarried extensively for granite setts used in roads across Britain.
The village sits dramatically between the mountain and the Irish Sea.
Prehistoric axe factories on the mountain date back around 4,000 years.
Llanfairfechan sits on the North Wales coast path, between Bangor and Conwy.
The village developed as a small Victorian seaside resort.
It looks out towards Puffin Island and the Isle of Anglesey.
Gwrych Castle, near Abergele, gained fame as the location for I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! in 2020 and 2021.
The castle was built in the 1810s in a dramatic mock-medieval style.
Abergele sits on the North Wales coast between Colwyn Bay and Rhyl.
Betws-y-Coed sits at the meeting point of three rivers in the heart of Eryri (Snowdonia).
The village became a popular retreat for landscape artists from the mid-19th century.
Nearby Conwy Falls and Swallow Falls are among the most visited waterfalls in Wales.
Llanrwst's elegant stone bridge, often attributed to Inigo Jones, dates from around 1636.
The town sits in the Conwy Valley, within Eryri (Snowdonia) National Park.
Llanrwst was historically an important market town for the Conwy Valley's farming community.
Morfa Mawddach sits at the mouth of the Mawddach Estuary, opposite Barmouth.
A footbridge alongside the railway viaduct allows walkers to cross the estuary.
The estuary is regarded as one of the most scenic in Wales.
Dyffryn Ardudwy has the remains of two Neolithic burial chambers, among the oldest structures in Wales.
The village sits on the coast between Harlech and Barmouth.
The area is rich in prehistoric monuments across the surrounding hills.
Pwllheli has held a market charter since 1355.
The town's harbour and marina are a base for exploring the Llyn Peninsula coastline.
Pwllheli is the western terminus of the Cambrian Coast Line.
At very low tides, an ancient submerged forest of preserved tree stumps is revealed on Borth beach, thousands of years old.
Borth has a long, straight beach backed by a shingle ridge.
The village sits on Cardigan Bay, close to the Dyfi Estuary.
Llandrindod Wells became a fashionable spa town after its mineral springs were promoted from the 1860s.
The town's Rock Park still has original Victorian spa buildings.
Llandrindod hosts an annual Victorian Festival celebrating its heritage.
Gobowen was once a major junction on the Cambrian Railways network.
Park Hall, nearby, offers a farm park and countryside attraction popular with families.
Gobowen sits close to the Shropshire-Wales border, near Oswestry.
Buckley was once a major centre of brick, tile and pottery manufacturing in North Wales.
The town sits on a ridge in Flintshire, with wide views over the Dee Estuary.
Buckley developed largely around its clay and coal deposits.
Prees sits in rural north Shropshire, close to the Welsh border.
The village has a history stretching back to Anglo-Saxon times, named in the Domesday Book.
Prees Heath, nearby, is a nature reserve important for a rare butterfly, the silver-studded blue.
